Choice probabilities for each test item, with human response counts

Source: R/evaluation.R
choice_probabilities.Rd

For each test item, returns the alternatives offered, the correct object, the model's probability of choosing each alternative, and how many participants chose each one. This is the full choice distribution behind the accuracy that xsl_run() scores: the probability of the correct alternative is exactly that item's entry in perf. It is what a multinomial likelihood (xslControl(objective = "multinomial")) compares with the data, and it shows which wrong objects a model expects learners to choose.

Usage

choice_probabilities(m, data, d = NULL, lapse = 0, block = NULL, phi = NULL)

Arguments

m

A word-by-object matrix, e.g. xsl_run(mod, data)$fits[[1]]$matrix.

data

The xslData condition m was learned from.

d

Optional choice exponent (a model's ch_dec; see get_perf()).

lapse

Lapse rate: the probability of guessing uniformly among the alternatives, mixed into p (0, the default, leaves p as the model's choice rule gives it).

block

For a multi-block condition, which block's responses to return (m should then be that block's matrix, e.g. xsl_run(mod, data)$fits[[1]]$blocks[[block]]$matrix).

phi

Optional softmax inverse temperature (a model's phi; see softmax_weights()). For a stochastic model, pass the mean matrix, matrix / n_sim, as xsl_run() scores it.

Value

A tibble with one row per test item: item, correct (the correct object's label), and list columns alternatives (object labels), p (choice probabilities over alternatives) and counts (participants choosing each alternative; NULL entries if data has no response_matrix).

Details

Items are scored as in xsl_run(): on a condition with a test, by Luce choice over each test trial's listed objects (see mafc_test()); otherwise among all objects, with word i's correct referent the i-th object (see get_perf()).

Examples

dat <- xsl_datasets[[1]]
fit <- xsl_run(uncfam(X = .1, B = 3, C = .97), dat)$fits[[1]]
ch <- choice_probabilities(fit$matrix, dat)
ch$p[[1]]       # the model's choice distribution for item 1
#>  [1] 0.42412064 0.03117284 0.05779498 0.03232234 0.03281867 0.01819889
#>  [7] 0.01876175 0.05414666 0.03658513 0.04601400 0.03447850 0.03281867
#> [13] 0.03848299 0.02629217 0.01819889 0.03374124 0.02055692 0.04349470
ch$counts[[1]]  # what participants chose
#>  [1] 7 3 2 0 0 0 2 0 0 0 1 1 1 0 2 3 2 1
